summary.text: From the defining sum one obtains the recurrence \(a(n+1)=2^{\binom{n+1}{2}}+(2^n-1)a(n)\); for odd prime \(p\), Fermat’s theorem together with \(\binom{n+2(p-1)+1}{2}-\binom{n+1}{2}=(2n+2p-1)(p-1)\) makes both powers of \(2\) in this recurrence invariant modulo \(p\) after the shift, while the base case follows because \(2^{2(p-1)}-1\equiv0\), so induction gives the result. For \(p=2\), the recurrence shows every \(a(n)\) with \(n\ge1\) is odd, yielding the required congruence.

full_proof.text:
Let
\[
a(n)=\sum_{k=0}^{n-1}2^{\binom{k+1}{2}}
       \prod_{j=k+1}^{n-1}(2^j-1) \qquad (n\geq 1).
\]
Here an empty product is understood to be 1. Since
\(\binom{k+1}{2}=k(k+1)/2\), this is exactly the sequence in the statement.
We prove that, for every prime \(p\) and every \(n\geq 1\),
\[
a(n+2(p-1))\equiv a(n)\pmod p.
\]

First we derive a recurrence for the sequence. In the sum defining
\(a(n+1)\), the term with \(k=n\) is
\[
2^{\binom{n+1}{2}},
\]
because its product is empty. For every term with \(0\leq k<n\), the product
from \(k+1\) through \(n\) is obtained from the corresponding product in
\(a(n)\) by adjoining the factor \(2^n-1\). Consequently
\[
\boxed{\quad a(n+1)=2^{\binom{n+1}{2}}+(2^n-1)a(n)\quad}                 \tag{1}
\]
for every \(n\geq 0\). Also, directly from the definition,
\[
a(1)=1.                                                               \tag{2}
\]

We first dispose of the prime \(p=2\). We claim that
\[
a(m)\equiv 1\pmod 2                                                   \tag{3}
\]
for every \(m\geq 1\). The assertion is true for \(m=1\) by (2). Suppose it
is true for some \(m\geq 1\). Since \(\binom{m+1}{2}\geq 1\), the first term
on the right side of (1) is even. Moreover, \(2^m-1\) is odd. Thus (1) gives
\[
a(m+1)\equiv 0+1\cdot a(m)\equiv 1\pmod 2.
\]
This proves (3) by induction. Hence, for every \(n\geq 1\), both \(a(n+2)\)
and \(a(n)\) are congruent to 1 modulo 2. Since
\(2(p-1)=2\) when \(p=2\), the desired result follows in this case.

Now let \(p>2\) be prime, and put
\[
M=2(p-1).
\]
We will show that the two coefficients occurring in recurrence (1) are
periodic modulo \(p\) when their index is increased by \(M\).

Because \(p\) is odd, 2 is nonzero modulo \(p\). Fermat's little theorem
therefore gives
\[
2^{p-1}\equiv 1\pmod p.
\]
In particular,
\[
2^M=2^{2(p-1)}\equiv 1\pmod p.                                        \tag{4}
\]
It follows immediately that, for every \(r\geq 0\),
\[
2^{r+M}-1
 =2^r2^M-1
 \equiv 2^r-1\pmod p.                                                  \tag{5}
\]

We also need periodicity of the additive power in (1). The relevant
triangular-number identity is
\[
\binom{r+M+1}{2}
 =\binom{r+1}{2}+(2r+2p-1)(p-1).                                      \tag{6}
\]
Indeed, since \(M=2(p-1)\), twice the difference of the two binomial
coefficients is
\[
\begin{aligned}
&(r+2(p-1)+1)(r+2(p-1))-r(r+1)\\
&\qquad=2(2r+2p-1)(p-1),
\end{aligned}
\]
and division by 2 gives (6). Therefore, again using Fermat's little theorem,
\[
\begin{aligned}
2^{\binom{r+M+1}{2}}
&=2^{\binom{r+1}{2}}
  2^{(2r+2p-1)(p-1)}\\
&=2^{\binom{r+1}{2}}
  \left(2^{p-1}\right)^{2r+2p-1}\\
&\equiv 2^{\binom{r+1}{2}}\pmod p.                                    \tag{7}
\end{aligned}
\]
Thus both the additive term and the multiplicative coefficient in (1) are
unchanged modulo \(p\) after shifting the recurrence index by \(M\).

It remains to establish the appropriate initial value for an induction. We
claim
\[
a(M+1)\equiv a(1)\pmod p.                                             \tag{8}
\]
Applying (1) at \(n=M\) gives
\[
a(M+1)=2^{\binom{M+1}{2}}+(2^M-1)a(M).
\]
By (4), the second summand is zero modulo \(p\). By (7) with \(r=0\),
\[
2^{\binom{M+1}{2}}
 \equiv 2^{\binom{1}{2}}
 =2^0=1\pmod p.
\]
Hence \(a(M+1)\equiv 1=a(1)\pmod p\), proving (8).

We now prove by induction on \(n\geq 1\) that
\[
a(n+M)\equiv a(n)\pmod p.                                             \tag{9}
\]
The base case \(n=1\) is (8). Assume (9) holds for some \(n\geq 1\). Applying
recurrence (1) first at \(n+M\) and then at \(n\), and using (7), (5), and the
induction hypothesis, yields
\[
\begin{aligned}
a(n+M+1)
&=2^{\binom{n+M+1}{2}}+(2^{n+M}-1)a(n+M)\\
&\equiv 2^{\binom{n+1}{2}}+(2^n-1)a(n)\\
&=a(n+1)\pmod p.
\end{aligned}
\]
This completes the induction and proves (9) for every \(n\geq 1\).
Substituting \(M=2(p-1)\) gives
\[
\boxed{a(n+2(p-1))\equiv a(n)\pmod p}
\]
for every prime \(p\) and every \(n\geq 1\), as required.
